minor: 'Because of them, Russia and Japan never signed a World War Two peace treaty' states the cause flatly. The sources only say no treaty was signed, and the Soviet refusal at San Francisco in 1951 is also part of the story. Consider 'Largely because of them'.
'Shinzo Abe went further than anyone' is an evaluation, not a sourced fact. The 27 meetings are sourced and attributed, so it could be cut to 'met Putin 27 times'.
'a step no Japanese government has publicly accepted' has no entry in the sources list. Add one or soften it.
'The largest town, Yuzhno-Kurilsk' has no listed source for 'largest'. The sources only establish it as the district seat.
'Moscow stopped blocking Japan's entry to the United Nations' is true, but the listed source gives only the 18 December 1956 admission date. Add a source for the earlier Soviet veto.
'On the map nothing would change' under shared use is an analyst-style projection. It is fine as 'analysts sketch', but keep it attributed.
'So the 1945 line held, and it is still the line on the water today, between Hokkaido and Kunashir' is slightly loose. The line runs between Hokkaido and all four islands, not only Kunashir.

shots.vo: The gap still shapes Japan's energy deals and Russia's submarine routes to the Pacific.
So who owns the Kuril Islands, and why is it unsettled after eight decades?
The answer starts on a winter day in 1855, at a port called Shimoda.

shots.vo: The Kuril chain runs about 1,200 kilometres from Hokkaido to Russia's Kamchatka peninsula, roughly 56 islands in all.
The dispute is about the four southernmost: Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the small Habomai group.
Japan calls them the Northern Territories, while Russia calls them the Southern Kurils, part of its Sakhalin region.

map.label: Japan: Northern Territories · Russia: Southern Kurils

shots.vo: Together they cover about 5,000 square kilometres, and Iturup alone makes up almost two thirds of that.

chart.title: Iturup dwarfs the rest
chart.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan

shots.vo: Kunashir lies about 16 kilometres from Hokkaido's Notsuke peninsula, close enough to see across the water on a clear day.
The Habomai islets are closer still, just 3.7 kilometres from Cape Nosappu, where Japanese visitors come to look across.
About 20,000 people live on the islands today, by Russian figures, mostly in small fishing towns and ports.

shots.vo: The largest town, Yuzhno-Kurilsk on Kunashir, is the seat of a district run from Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, far to the west.
Around them lie some of the North Pacific's richest fishing grounds, where a cold current meets a warm one.
Between the islands run deep straits that link the Sea of Okhotsk with the open Pacific Ocean.
Defence analysts describe the Sea of Okhotsk as a protected zone for Russia's missile submarines in the Pacific.
In 2016 Russia's defence ministry announced coastal missile systems on Iturup and Kunashir, facing the straits.
Seen from Tokyo, the islands are lost homes; seen from Moscow, they guard a door to an ocean.
And the line Japan claims today was first drawn by both countries together, 171 years ago.

shots.vo: In February 1855 a Russian envoy, Vice Admiral Yevfimy Putyatin, sat down with Japanese officials at Shimoda.
On 7 February Putyatin and the shogun's envoys, Kawaji Toshiakira and Tsutsui Masanori, signed a treaty setting the Iturup-Urup border.

document.title: Treaty of Shimoda, 7 February 1855
document.highlight: Henceforth the boundary between the two nations shall lie between the islands of Etorofu and Uruppu.

shots.prompt: Duotone plate, dark slate and muted orange: an old treaty scroll and seal on a lacquered desk by lamplight, top third plain dark

shots.vo: Everything from Iturup southward went to Japan, while Urup and the islands above it went to Russia.
Sakhalin, the long island to the west, was left undivided, open to settlers from both countries.
Twenty years later, in 1875, Japan gave up its claims on Sakhalin in exchange for every Kuril island.
Japan's border now ran right up to Shumshu, within sight of the southern cape of Kamchatka.
After the Russo-Japanese War, a 1905 treaty signed in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, gave Japan southern Sakhalin as well.
So by 1945 the map had moved three times by treaty, and the fourth move would come through war.
In February 1945 at Yalta in Crimea, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agreed terms for Soviet entry into the war against Japan.
Their secret agreement said, in a single line, that the Kuril islands shall be handed over to the Soviet Union.

quote.text: The Kuril islands shall be handed over to the Soviet Union.
quote.who: Yalta Agreement, signed by Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin

shots.vo: Japan was not at Yalta, and it has long said that a deal made without it cannot bind it.

They moved down the chain, reaching Iturup on 28 August and Kunashir and Shikotan by 1 September.
The Habomai islets were taken between 3 and 5 September, after Japan had formally signed its surrender.
Some 17,291 Japanese lived on the four islands, and by 1949 all of them had been sent to Japan.

shots.vo: Japan's position is that Iturup and Kunashir were never Kuriles in that sense, and Habomai and Shikotan belong to Hokkaido.
The Soviet delegation attended in San Francisco but refused to sign, so Moscow and Tokyo still had no treaty at all.

shots.vo: In October 1956, Prime Minister Ichiro Hatoyama travelled to Moscow to end the state of war.
The Joint Declaration, signed on 19 October by Hatoyama and Soviet Premier Bulganin, restored relations and promised Japan two islands.

document.title: Joint Declaration by the USSR and Japan, 19 October 1956
document.highlight: Article 9: the Soviet Union agrees to transfer to Japan the Habomai Islands and the island of Shikoten.

quote.text: ...provided, however, that the actual transfer of these islands to Japan shall take place after the conclusion of a Peace Treaty

shots.vo: On the map, that would have put the border between Shikotan and Kunashir, leaving Russia the two larger islands.
Habomai and Shikotan add up to only 348 square kilometres, about seven percent of the land Japan claims.
Both parliaments ratified it, and in December 1956 Moscow stopped blocking Japan's entry to the United Nations.

map.label: Shikotan-Kunashir line ratified, Dec 1956 · Japan joins UN, 18 Dec

shots.vo: But Japan held out for all four islands, and historians such as Kimie Hara say American pressure played a part.
By those accounts, in August 1956 US Secretary of State John Foster Dulles linked a Japanese concession to Okinawa, then under US control.
Four years later, after Japan renewed its security treaty with Washington, Moscow added a condition of its own.
A Soviet note in January 1960 said the two islands would be handed over only after foreign troops left Japan.

map.label: 1956 line: only if foreign troops leave (27 Jan 1960)

shots.vo: So the 1945 line held, and it is still the line on the water today, between Hokkaido and Kunashir.
Leaders on both sides have tried to move it ever since, and every one of them has stopped short—why?

shots.vo: The talks never really stopped: Tokyo in 1993, Irkutsk in 2001 and Singapore in 2018 each promised progress on a treaty.
In the 1993 Tokyo Declaration, Boris Yeltsin and Morihiro Hosokawa named all four islands as the question to settle.

shots.vo: In 2001 at Irkutsk, Vladimir Putin and Yoshiro Mori confirmed the 1956 declaration as the legal starting point.
In November 2010 Dmitry Medvedev became the first Russian leader to visit the islands, landing on Kunashir.
Shinzo Abe went further than anyone, meeting Putin 27 times as prime minister, according to Japanese press counts.

shots.vo: In Singapore in November 2018, the two leaders agreed to speed up talks on the basis of the 1956 declaration.
Japanese newspapers widely read that as a shift toward two islands first, while the government said its position was unchanged.
Russia's case, at its strongest, is that the islands became Soviet lawfully, as an agreed result of the Second World War.
Its foreign ministry points to Yalta, to Japan's renunciation in 1951, and to Article 107 of the UN Charter.

document.title: Charter of the United Nations, Article 107 (1945)
document.highlight: Nothing in the present Charter shall invalidate or preclude action... taken or authorized as a result of that war by the Governments having responsibility for such action.

In 2020 Russia amended its constitution to forbid any action aimed at giving away part of its territory.

document.highlight: Actions aimed at the alienation of part of the territory of the Russian Federation are not permitted (border delimitation excepted).

shots.vo: Japan's case, at its strongest, is that these four islands had never been Russian until Soviet troops arrived in 1945.
Tokyo points to the 1855 line, drawn by both countries in peace, and to the Neutrality Pact it says was broken.
Then there are the people: 17,291 Japanese lived there in 1945, and about 20,000 Russian citizens live there now.
From 1964 Japanese families could visit graves on the islands, and from 1992 residents on both sides made visa-free visits.
The surviving former Japanese islanders now number only a few thousand, with an average age close to 90.
Then on 21 March 2022 Russia suspended the peace treaty talks, after Japan joined sanctions over the war in Ukraine.

shots.vo: Moscow also halted the visa-free visits, cutting the last regular human link across the 1945 line.
Yet business has not fully stopped: Japan's Mitsui and Mitsubishi kept their stakes in the Sakhalin-2 gas project.
Its tankers load in southern Sakhalin and reach Japan through La Pérouse Strait, west of the disputed islands.

shots.vo: In 2018 Russia stationed fighter jets at Iturup's airfield, and Japan protested, as it has at other deployments.
So the line is frozen, both cases are fixed in law, and the talks are stopped; what could move it now?
Analysts usually sketch three possible outcomes, and each one would draw a different line across this water.
The first is the 1956 deal: Habomai and Shikotan would go to Japan, and a peace treaty would be signed.
The new border would run through the strait between Shikotan and Kunashir, leaving the deep northern straits in Russian hands.
Russia would keep Iturup and Kunashir, about 93 percent of the land, and the straits between them.
For Japan it would mean giving up the claim to the larger islands, a step no Japanese government has publicly accepted.

shots.vo: The second outcome is the one on the map now: the 1945 line simply stays, and no treaty is signed.
Under a 1998 agreement Japanese boats fish near the islands, and Russia suspended it in June 2022 in a dispute over payments.
That outcome would leave them without a treaty for as long as it lasts.

shots.vo: The third is some form of shared use: joint fishing, tourism and farming on the islands, with sovereignty set aside.
Abe and Putin agreed at Nagato in December 2016 to work toward exactly that, joint economic activity on all four islands.
Pilot projects in fish farming, greenhouses and tourism were listed in 2017, and a few Japanese tourist trips ran in 2019.
On the map nothing would change, but Japanese boats and visitors could cross the line under a special legal regime.
The obstacle has been law itself: neither side has found a way for its citizens to work there under the other's rules.

shots.vo: Analysts say which outcome comes first, if any, may depend on events far from these islands, including the war in Ukraine.

shots.vo: Eighty years on, the Kurils are not really missing a border; they are missing a signature both capitals can accept.
If you were drawing this map, where would your line go: the line of 1855, of 1956, or of 1945?
Next, another line Russia watches closely: the Suwałki Gap, the narrow strip of land between Poland and Lithuania.
